correctness.rationale: The centered graphical zonotope has the exact cut halfspace description |sum_{i in S}x_i|<=|delta S|/2, justified by coarea/support-function separation. Thus a radius r ball at c is feasible iff |sum_S c_i|+r sqrt(|S|(n-|S|)/n)<=|delta S|/2. For C_n^2 every singleton cut has size four; six-edge cyclic intervals/distance-two pairs and all remaining >=8 are classified by circular bit-change counting. Comparing normalized singleton and balanced cuts gives radius 2sqrt(n/(n-1)) for n6,7, 3sqrt(n/floor(n²/4)) for n>=8. Tight singleton/length-m cuts force the claimed unique odd centers or the repeated vector (y,y) for even n. Singleton and near-balanced intervals respectively give gamma_m=2-3sqrt(2m-1)/m and beta_m=3(1-sqrt(1-1/m²)); min is gamma_4 and beta_m for m>=5. For general center candidates, convexity of f_m(d)=3(1-sqrt(1-d²/m²)) dominates d beta_m; all large-cut slack >=1 while m b_m<1, proving sufficiency for every cut, not just identified facets. The hyperplane cube-section vertex count follows m-1 active coordinate bounds. Fresh independent exact cut enumeration for n6..12 corroborates active normal families and radius; infinite n follows symbolic inequalities, not a bounded census.

value.rationale: The center locus of a maximal Euclidean inball is a natural geometric invariant of a graphical zonotope, not fixed by its scalar inradius. The exact parity phenomenon, its first exceptional n=8 transition between two distinct active-cut types, sharp coordinate bounds and vertex census form a meaningful complete classification for the canonical second power of the cycle. The analogy with ordinary cycles makes the exceptional transition particularly informative.

final_claim: For the centered intrinsic-Euclidean zonotope of squared cycle C_n^2 (n>=6) all maximum-inscribed-ball centers are uniquely zero for n=6,7 and odd n>=9; for even n=2m>=8 the locus is {(y,y):sum y_i=0, |y_i|<=b_m}, b4=2-3sqrt7/4 and b_m=3(1-sqrt(1-1/m^2)) for m>=5. Sharp transition at eight vertices; explicit dimension m-1 and cube-section vertex counts. Inradius follows earlier general cut formula.
